article.title: DSA SF’s Battle for an Affordable, Equitable San Francisco
article.author: San Francisco DSA
article.content: The Democratic Socialists of America won 160 elected offices and ballot measures across the country this month. One of those measures, Proposition B for a San Francisco Public Bank, has been added to the list of DSA SF’s electoral victories. In red states and blue, the message of these midterms was clear: Working people want socialism. However, here at home, our oligarch mayor and his billionaire friends spent record sums to convince San Francisco voters to amend the city charter in order to consolidate control in the Mayor’s Office and limit working class access to the ballot. Socialists, as part of the broader working class movement, went toe to toe with the new San Francisco machine – the coalition of corporate real estate and tech money that has formed around Mayor Lurie – to fight for a San Francisco where everyone can afford to live and thrive, at a time when rents and evictions are rising exponentially without any end or meaningful intervention in sight. Prop I: Affordable Housing Guarantee Act Prop I would have introduced the largest increase in affordable housing production in years, dedicating an average of $120 million each year to housing working families can afford by permanently dedicating revenue from an existing tax on the sale of mansions and skyscrapers to social and affordable housing, rent relief, and eviction defense. Billionaires and corporate landlords spent $2.8 million on a misinformation campaign supported by Mayor Lurie, the San Francisco Chronicle editorial board, and dark money influencers like GrowSF to convince San Franciscans that they should vote against affordable housing. They needed every penny. We mobilized thousands of volunteers, reached 250,000 voters, and earned 48% of the vote against the full might of the machine. While we narrowly lost on election day, Prop I scored a major victory months before the first vote was cast. We brought this measure as a response to Mayor Lurie and Supervisor Bilal Mahmood’s BUILD Act, which proposed to repeal the transfer tax increase that our chapter won at the ballot in 2020. Not only did our pressure contribute to the mayor’s abandonment of that policy in 2026, our campaign momentum forced him into a tacit pledge that transfer tax repeal is off the table. Mayor Lurie dearly wants to give real estate speculators a tax break and call it a housing policy, but now he is on the record saying that doing so would “blow a hole in our city’s budget” taking away “money that could be used for firefighters, public safety, and cleaning our streets.” While the loss of Prop I continues the status quo, it is up to us to hold City Hall accountable to using money collected from Prop I passed in 2020 toward building housing and demand they do so. Through the Prop I campaign, we built bridges with a strong coalition of public sector workers including SEIU 1021 and IFPTE Local 21, the United Educators of San Francisco, tenant organizations, and affordable housing advocates. We knocked doors across buildings in SOMA and the Tenderloin to campaign for Prop I and spread the word about tenants’ rights. Through advocacy, urgent action, and organizing alongside our coalition partners, we will continue to fight for the belief that housing is a human right. We will ensure that publicly-owned social housing is created, and fight the near-constant attempts by real estate speculators and corporate landlords to take over San Francisco. Join this work by coming to an upcoming meeting of our Social Housing or Tenant Organizing working groups. Prop B for a Public Bank The decade-long, DSA SF-led movement for a San Francisco Public Bank scored a historic victory with the passage of Proposition B, which authorizes the functions and governance of the nation’s first municipal public bank. As enabled by Prop B, the San Francisco Public Bank will be a financial institution that prioritizes the public good over private profit to fund the things our city needs most: social and affordable housing, green infrastructure, and local small businesses. And it will do so while keeping our money out of the Wall Street banks which fund climate destruction and imperialism. San Francisco’s Prop B is the first measure of its kind, asking voters to demand a municipal city-owned public bank. The road to Prop B has been a long one: DSA SF’s socialist in office, Supervisor Jackie Fielder, founded the SF Public Bank Coalition in 2017 to establish alternative financing opportunities to achieve maximum local impact. For nearly ten years, the coalition has been driven by working-class people of color deeply embedded in our communities. The grassroots coalition brought together climate justice advocates and community organizers to bring the issue of a public bank to local and regional lawmakers, paving the way to this historic victory. Though it was opposed by corporate interests, dark money groups, and our own Mayor, the coalition was able to beat back misinformation and garner support from a broad coalition of labor and progressive organizations. Alongside the Public Bank Coalition, DSA SF mobilized thousands of volunteers, solicited support from neighborhood groups, and canvassed households across San Francisco to educate and inspire support for a public bank. This win is a lesson in steadfastness—no matter how long it takes, we will continue to fight for the socialist future we all deserve. And it is only through grassroots local organizing efforts that we can win socialist policies like local democratized financing. The passage of Prop B proves San Franciscans are ready to move past traditional capitalist lending strategies that have failed to deliver for our communities. Rather than fill the coffers of Wall Street banks, San Franciscans chose to set an example of community wealth building and the creation of resilient local economies that work for the common good. DSA SF is proud to earn this victory alongside the SF Public Bank Coalition for the people of San Francisco. Join a meeting of our Ecosocialism Working Group to learn about the next steps toward public bank formation and how you can help. Socialists for Schools: Bunny McFadden and Reina Tello We are committed to launching grassroots organizers as candidates. DSA SF also endorsed two longtime grassroots organizers who ran to fight for public education that serves the working class. School board races in San Francisco have long been marred by recalls and PAC-spending. Bunny McFadden and Reina Tello proudly ran as socialists in the City College Board of Trustees and School Board races, respectively. McFadden and Tello were able to garner endorsements from unions, including the United Educators of San Francisco and American Federation of Teachers Local 2121, democratic clubs, and current and former Supervisors from across the City. Both McFadden and Tello ran strong campaigns and never compromised their values. They brought the fight to corporate-backed candidates and ultimately gained the support of working-class families, students, and teachers. We hope their races can build the framework for future grassroots organizers competing for offices like the San Francisco School Board: a post that has historically been used by elites backed by dark money groups to launch the careers of candidates who will carry out the will of corporate interests. Despite these losses, DSA SF is committed to the struggle for public education that supports students and faculty in our city. With rank-and-file members like McFadden and Tello, we know we can continue to build power with students, teachers, and working families to expand public resources like Free City College and win the highest quality public education for our students. No on D, E, F: Opposing the Mayor’s Power Grab We will always fight for the working class to govern, and struggle for a new political system. DSA SF has led grassroots campaigns that triumph at the ballot box, like passing the tenant right to counsel and taxing wealthy real estate speculators to fund affordable housing. This is no doubt why the Mayor’s billionaire allies and astro-turfing groups like GrowSF devoted millions to passing Prop D to limit our democracy. We’ve elected socialist candidates Harry Britt, Dean Preston and Jackie Fielder to the Board of Supervisors to provide critical oversight of the Mayor’s policies and appointees. So, it’s no surprise the Mayor’s allies launched a well-funded misinformation campaign to convince voters that Prop E and Prop F would stop corruption in City Hall—when, in fact, they just centralize power in the Mayor’s office and limit Board oversight. Lurie’s billionaire allies raised over $13.2 million to pass these measures, more than any ballot measure committee in San Francisco history. The success of their power grab absolutely hinders our goal to have working-class people shape City government. It also eliminates any excuses. While his approval rating remains high by some standards, his self-described “moderate” policies mirror the authoritarian, anti-working-class policies of the Republican Party. Conditions for working people have deteriorated on Lurie’s watch: housing costs have skyrocketed thanks to his prioritization of corporate real estate profits. In June, he cut social services, including LGTBQ healthcare and senior care, leaving vacancies across critical departments like Public Health. The Mayor’s massive private PR spending and billionaire alliance can only suspend voters’ disbelief for so long while San Franciscans continue to suffer the consequences of his laissez-faire policies. Across the country, everyday people voted against data centers, mass surveillance, and electeds who support U.S. funding of the ongoing genocide in Palestine — the very things the San Francisco Democratic Party has come to stand for. It’s Up to Us DSA is a fabric of organizers pushing in different lanes toward the same goal: winning socialism. This election is just one small fraction of the continued fight against the entire global system of capital that pits working class people against each other to ensure the rich get richer and stay in power. At its heart, democratic socialism is a movement to provide what all workers want: less of their days spent working and worrying about the bills; healthy homes and families that are cared for; real democratic representation; and a world where we labor for the common good instead of private profit and domination. We push these demands to their furthest extent today, and fight to realize a socialist future tomorrow. The only path forward is to join together with other working San Franciscans committed to winning the world we deserve. If you haven’t yet joined, now is the time to do so. Join us at dsasf.org/join .
